title: Male Urethral Catheterisation - Procedure Explanation
patient_instructions: You are a final-year medical student attached to the Emergency Department (the candidate is teaching/explaining to you). The next patient is a man in acute urinary retention who needs an indwelling urinary catheter. Your role is to listen and to ask clarifying questions so the candidate can demonstrate a clear, structured explanation. Prompts you may use if the candidate is vague: 'How do you keep it sterile?', 'What size catheter do you use and why?', 'What do you inflate the balloon with?', 'What are the risks I should mention when consenting the patient?', 'Is there anyone we should NOT catheterise?', 'What do you document afterwards?'. Affect: keen, engaged, note-taking. You do not know the answers yourself; you rely on the candidate to teach you.
candidate_instructions: You are the resident in the Emergency Department. A patient has presented in acute urinary retention and requires urethral catheterisation. Task: explain the catheterisation procedure to your medical student. Cover consent and chaperone, screening for contraindications, equipment and catheter selection, aseptic technique and hand hygiene, the insertion steps, balloon inflation, post-procedure care and safety-netting, and documentation. You are teaching the student, not performing the procedure on a patient.
examiner_instructions: Assess the candidate as a teacher: is the explanation logical, complete and safe? Expect informed consent (explained, obtained, documented), offer of a chaperone, and explanation of risks (UTI, urethral injury/false passage, bleeding, latex/material allergy). Critically, the candidate should screen for contraindications BEFORE instrumenting the urethra - blood at the meatus, perineal/scrotal bruising, high-riding or non-palpable prostate, or pelvic trauma mandate urology review, not forcing a catheter. Reward that this is an aseptic non-touch technique (ANTT) with standard hand hygiene (alcohol rub 20-30 s or wash 40-60 s), NOT a 2-minute surgical scrub. Reward correct catheter selection (14-16 Fr standard; 18-22 Fr or three-way if haematuria/clots), balloon inflated with STERILE WATER (not saline), and post-procedure monitoring for post-obstructive diuresis. Prompt if needed: 'Is there anyone you should not catheterise?'

criteria: Structured introduction and clear teaching approach to the student
Explains informed consent must be explained, obtained and documented
Offers a chaperone (required for a procedure on private parts, regardless of gender concordance)
Explains required exposure, privacy and dignity
Correct catheter selection (14-16 Fr standard; larger bore/three-way if haematuria) with rationale
Explains aseptic non-touch technique and correct hand-hygiene standard (not a surgical scrub)
Describes insertion steps and balloon inflation with STERILE WATER only if urine flows
Screens for and names contraindications (blood at meatus, perineal bruising, pelvic trauma, abnormal prostate) - do not force; seek urology review
Explains risks/complications (UTI, urethral injury/false passage, bleeding, allergy)
Post-procedure safety-net: monitor for post-obstructive diuresis, chart hourly output, secure catheter and connect drainage bag
Clear, logically sequenced, jargon-appropriate teaching that checks the student's understanding
Covers documentation (consent, indication, catheter type/size, balloon volume, residual volume, complications, specimen)

red_flags: Blood at the urethral meatus, perineal or scrotal bruising, or a high-riding/non-palpable prostate - signs of urethral injury; do NOT force a catheter, obtain urology review and consider retrograde urethrogram or suprapubic catheter
Inflating the balloon before confirming urine flow, or before the catheter is fully advanced - risk of urethral rupture and false passage
Failure to monitor for post-obstructive diuresis after draining a large residual volume (output >200 mL/hr requires fluid replacement)
Using normal saline instead of sterile water for balloon inflation (saline can crystallise and block the valve, trapping the catheter)
australian_guidelines: Hand Hygiene Australia '5 Moments': perform standard hand hygiene with alcohol-based hand rub (20-30 s) or soap-and-water wash (40-60 s) before donning sterile gloves - a timed surgical scrub is not required for catheterisation.
ACSQHC / NSW Health CAUTI-prevention bundle: use aseptic non-touch technique, select the smallest appropriate catheter, avoid unnecessary catheterisation and remove promptly.
Therapeutic Guidelines: aqueous chlorhexidine (or sterile saline if chlorhexidine allergy) for meatal cleaning; use lignocaine gel and maintain an aseptic field throughout.
learning_objectives: Obtain and document informed consent and offer a chaperone for an intimate procedure.
Screen for contraindications to urethral catheterisation before instrumenting the urethra.
Describe aseptic non-touch technique and correct hand-hygiene standards.
Select the correct catheter and inflation fluid and describe safe insertion.
Provide post-procedure monitoring including recognition of post-obstructive diuresis, and document appropriately.
key_points: Catheterisation is an aseptic non-touch technique, not a sterile surgical operation - standard hand hygiene suffices.
Always exclude urethral injury before catheterising; blood at the meatus or pelvic trauma is a contraindication.
Standard adult male catheter is 14-16 Fr; use 18-22 Fr or a three-way catheter for frank haematuria/clot retention.
Inflate the balloon with sterile water only, and only after urine flows.
After draining a large residual, watch for post-obstructive diuresis and replace fluids if output exceeds 200 mL/hr.

citations.claim: The station assesses consultancy/procedural and communication competencies (consent, explanation, aseptic technique, documentation), which are core AMC domains.
Indication for catheterisation includes bladder outlet obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia and urethral stricture causing retention.
A structured, examiner-scored procedural performance-guideline framework underpins the demonstration of a clinical skill.
